```{r, include = FALSE}
have_rms <- requireNamespace("rms", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = have_rms
)

build_rich_tables <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
have_me <- have_rms && requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)
have_gt <- have_rms && requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
have_clubsw <- have_rms && requireNamespace("clubSandwich", quietly = TRUE)
source("_pkgdown-helpers.R")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(spicy)
library(rms) # lrm(), ols(), Glm(), cph(), rcs(), datadist()
library(survival) # Surv(), pbc
```

This article covers models fitted with the rms package (Harrell,
2015): `lrm()` for logistic regression, `ols()` for the linear model,
`Glm()` for generalized linear models and `cph()` for the Cox model.
The companion article [*Publication-ready regression
tables*](table-regression.html) covers the shared mechanics (output
engines, labels, `tidy()`). An `lrm()` fit of an ordinal outcome is a
proportional-odds model, and its table has the thresholds block
described in [*Ordinal regression
tables*](table-regression-ordinal.html). The
class-by-class map is [*Supported
models*](table-regression-supported-models.html).

## What an rms fit is for

The fitting functions of rms estimate the same models as `lm()`,
`glm()` and `coxph()`. An analyst chooses them for what comes with the
fit: spline terms declared in the formula, `anova()` tests that pool
all the terms of a predictor, `summary()` and `Predict()` for effects
over a chosen range, and the validation, calibration and nomogram
tools of the package.

`table_regression()` reads the fit as it is and builds the table a
paper needs. The estimates and their standard errors are those of rms.

## The data

The examples use the Pima diabetes data of MASS (Venables & Ripley,
2002): 532 women of Pima heritage aged 21 or more, tested for
diabetes, of whom 177 are diabetic. The training and the test halves
of MASS are stacked. One question runs through the article: is age
associated with diabetes at equal glucose, body mass index and number
of pregnancies, and is that association linear?

```{r data}
pima <- rbind(MASS::Pima.tr, MASS::Pima.te)
dd <- datadist(pima)
options(datadist = "dd")
c(n = nrow(pima), diabetic = sum(pima$type == "Yes"))
```

`datadist()` is a requirement of rms's own `summary()` and
`Predict()`. `table_regression()` does not need it.

## A first table

```{r first-table}
fit_lin <- lrm(type ~ age + bmi + glu + npreg, data = pima)
table_regression(fit_lin)
```

The coefficients and the standard errors are those of
`print(fit_lin)`, rounded: 0.0264 (0.0131) for age prints as
0.03 (0.01). The tests are Wald z tests, as in rms.

The fit statistics differ from rms's printout. The table reports
Tjur's (2009) and McFadden's R² and the AIC, which `print()` does not
show. It leaves out the likelihood-ratio χ² of the model and the
indexes of discrimination and accuracy (C, D~xy~, the Brier score),
which have no token. A later section carries two of them, the C index
and the Brier score, in the note.

## The same model as `glm()`

```{r glm-twin}
fit_glm <- glm(type ~ age + bmi + glu + npreg, data = pima, family = binomial)

table_regression(
  list(glm = fit_glm, lrm = fit_lin),
  digits = 4,
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

The two columns agree to four decimals, and so do the fit statistics:
`lrm()` and `glm()` maximize the same likelihood. A table can
therefore hold fits of both engines when an analysis used each for a
part of its models.

## Relaxing linearity: restricted cubic splines

The linear model assumes that each year of age shifts the log-odds by
the same amount. Harrell advises against assuming it for a continuous
predictor without a reason: "Relationships among variables are seldom
linear" (Harrell, 2015, p. 18). A restricted cubic spline lets the
data choose the shape. It is a piecewise cubic function, constrained
to be linear beyond the outer knots, and it costs k − 1 coefficients
for k knots (p. 24).

```{r spline}
fit_rcs <- lrm(
  type ~ rcs(age, 4) + bmi + glu + npreg,
  data = pima, x = TRUE, y = TRUE
)
fit_rcs$Design$parms$age
table_regression(fit_rcs)
```

With four knots, rms places them at the 5th, 35th, 65th and 95th
percentiles of age: 21, 25, 33 and 54 years. `x = TRUE, y = TRUE`
stores the design matrix and the response in the fit, for the robust
variance and the penalized fit of later sections.

The table has three rows for age, named as rms names them: `age`,
`age'` and `age''`. None of them reads alone. They are the
coefficients of three basis functions, and the p-value of one row
tests one basis function with the two others kept in the model, which
answers no question about age. Two questions do have an answer: is
age associated with diabetes at all, and does the association depart
from a line?

## Testing a predictor as a whole

Each question compares two nested models, and `nested = TRUE` puts
the comparison in the table. Harrell gives the order: "all terms
involving the predictor should be tested simultaneously to check
whether the factor is associated with the outcome. This test should
precede the test for linearity" (p. 32).

```{r joint-tests}
fit_noage <- lrm(type ~ bmi + glu + npreg, data = pima)

table_regression(
  list("Without age" = fit_noage, "Spline" = fit_rcs),
  nested = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "aic", "lrt_change", "p_change")
)

table_regression(
  list(Linear = fit_lin, Spline = fit_rcs),
  nested = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "aic", "lrt_change", "p_change")
)
```

The first table tests the three age coefficients together: Δχ² =
18.57 on 3 degrees of freedom, p < .001. Age is associated with
diabetes. The second tests the two nonlinear coefficients: Δχ² =
14.46 on 2 degrees of freedom, p < .001. The association is not
linear.

Both are likelihood-ratio tests. `anova(fit_rcs)` of rms gives the
Wald version of the same two hypotheses, 17.60 and 13.64 here, with
the same conclusions.

## How many knots

Harrell reports that the fit depends on the number of knots much more
than on their position, and that four knots suit many data sets
(p. 26, 28). The AIC can arbitrate.

```{r knots}
sapply(3:5, function(k) {
  f <- lrm(type ~ rcs(age, k) + bmi + glu + npreg, data = pima)
  c(knots = k, AIC = round(AIC(f), 1))
})
```

Three knots have the lowest AIC, four are about one point above, and a
fifth adds a coefficient for nothing. The article keeps four.

## Reading a nonlinear effect

A table holds one number per predictor, and a curve does not fit in
one number. The average marginal effect is the closest summary: the
average, over the women of the sample, of the slope of the predicted
probability with respect to age.

```{r ame, eval = have_me}
table_regression(
  fit_rcs,
  show_columns = c("b", "ame", "ame_ci", "ame_p"),
  digits = 3
)
```

The AME of age appears once, on the first of its three rows, and it
takes the whole spline into account: 0.012, that is 1.2 percentage
points per year of age, 95% CI [0.006, 0.018]. The linear model gave
0.004.

The average hides the shape. `Predict()` of rms shows it, for a woman
with the median values of the other predictors:

```{r ame-shape}
Predict(fit_rcs, age = c(25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60), fun = plogis)
```

The predicted probability rises from 0.16 at 25 to 0.37 at 40, then
falls back to 0.25 at 60. A positive average slope summarizes a rise
followed by a decline, which is why the curve of a spline effect
belongs in the paper next to the table.

## Why not cut age into classes

Cutting a continuous predictor into classes is the common
alternative, and Harrell's judgment of it is blunt: "Nothing could
be more disastrous" (p. 19). Classes assume that the risk is flat
within each interval and jumps at its limits.

```{r categorize}
pima$age_group <- cut(pima$age, c(20, 30, 40, 50, 90), right = FALSE)
fit_cat <- lrm(type ~ age_group + bmi + glu + npreg, data = pima)

table_regression(
  list(Linear = fit_lin, Categories = fit_cat, Spline = fit_rcs),
  show_columns = c("b", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", "aic")
)
```

Four classes and a spline with four knots both spend three
coefficients on age. The classes reach an AIC of 487.7, the spline
480.7.

## Fit statistics

By default the table of an `lrm()` fit has the number of
observations, Tjur's R² for a binary outcome, McFadden's R² and the
AIC. The R² that rms prints is Nagelkerke's (1991), available as
`"pseudo_r2_nagelkerke"`.

```{r fit-stats}
table_regression(
  fit_rcs,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c(
    "nobs", "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", "pseudo_r2_tjur",
    "aic", "bic", "deviance", "log_lik"
  )
)
```

rms also computes indexes of discrimination and accuracy, kept in
`fit$stats`: the C index, Somers' D~xy~, the Brier score. They have
no token in `show_fit_stats`, and `note_add` carries them under the
table.

```{r fit-stats-note}
table_regression(
  fit_rcs,
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", "aic"),
  note_add = sprintf(
    "C index = %.3f; Brier score = %.3f (apparent, not validated).",
    fit_rcs$stats[["C"]], fit_rcs$stats[["Brier"]]
  )
)
```

These indexes are apparent: computed on the data that fitted the
model, they are optimistic. `rms::validate()` estimates the optimism
by bootstrap, and the corrected values are the ones to report.

## Odds ratios

`exponentiate = TRUE` turns the coefficients into odds ratios. The
rows of the spline are best left out: the exponential of a basis
coefficient is the odds ratio of nothing.

```{r odds-ratios}
table_regression(
  fit_rcs,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  drop = "age"
)
```

For age, `summary()` of rms compares two values of the predictor, by
default its quartiles.

```{r odds-ratios-age}
summary(fit_rcs)
```

The quartiles of age are 23 and 38 years. The odds of diabetes at 38
are 4.42 times those at 23, 95% CI [2.15, 9.08]. `note_add` can carry
that sentence under the table.

## Robust and bootstrap variance

rms computes the Huber sandwich with `robcov()` and a bootstrap
covariance matrix with `bootcov()`, each with optional clusters
(Harrell, 2015, p. 198). There are two ways to bring them into the
table.

The first is to ask `table_regression()`. `vcov = "CR0"` with a
`cluster` calls `robcov()` on the fit, which must have been fitted
with `x = TRUE, y = TRUE`. With one woman per cluster, the result is
the heteroskedasticity-robust sandwich.

```{r robust}
pima$id <- seq_len(nrow(pima))

table_regression(
  fit_rcs,
  vcov = "CR0",
  cluster = ~id,
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

The second is to pass a fit that already carries its variance.
`robcov()` and `bootcov()` return the fit with a new covariance
matrix. The table reports that matrix, and the note names the
estimator of each column.

```{r robust-own}
set.seed(2026)
fit_boot <- bootcov(fit_rcs, B = 200)

table_regression(
  list(Model = fit_rcs, Sandwich = robcov(fit_rcs), Bootstrap = fit_boot),
  show_columns = c("b", "se"),
  drop = "age"
)
```

The sandwich of `robcov()` is the Huber estimator, which is `CR0`. The
other tokens of `vcov` are refused, and the error says why.

```{r robust-refusal, error = TRUE}
table_regression(fit_rcs, vcov = "CR2", cluster = ~id)
```

## Penalized estimation

When a model has many coefficients for its sample, rms can shrink
them by penalized maximum likelihood. `pentrace()` searches the
penalty that optimizes an information criterion, and `update()`
refits with it.

```{r penalized}
pen <- pentrace(fit_rcs, seq(0, 20, by = 2))
pen$penalty
fit_pen <- update(fit_rcs, penalty = pen$penalty)

table_regression(
  list(MLE = fit_rcs, PMLE = fit_pen),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", "aic")
)
```

The penalty chosen is 2. The second column holds the penalized maximum
likelihood estimates (PMLE), and the note says so. Its standard errors
and p-values come from the covariance matrix that rms stores for a
penalized fit. Harrell warns about them: "Penalization will bias
estimates of β, so hypothesis tests and confidence intervals using
β̂^P^ may not have a simple interpretation" (p. 211). The penalized
column serves prediction. Tests are read in the unpenalized one.

The AIC of the penalized column is computed on the log-likelihood
without the penalty term, with the effective degrees of freedom, as
the note says. This is the criterion `pentrace()` optimizes, written on
the usual scale, where the lower value is the better one: 479.6 for the
penalized model against 480.7. `AIC(fit_pen)` of rms gives another
number, because it keeps the penalty term in the likelihood.

## `ols()` and `Glm()`

`ols()` is the linear model. Its table has the layout of an `lm()`
table, with t tests on the residual degrees of freedom, and a
hierarchy of `ols()` fits is compared by the F test of the change, as
for `lm()`.

```{r ols}
fit_ols_lin <- ols(bmi ~ age + npreg, data = pima)
fit_ols <- ols(bmi ~ rcs(age, 4) + npreg, data = pima)

table_regression(
  list(Linear = fit_ols_lin, Spline = fit_ols),
  nested = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "p")
)
```

The body mass index is not linear in age either: F = 11.28 on 2 and
527 degrees of freedom, the value `anova(fit_ols)` gives for the
nonlinear terms.

`Glm()` is `glm()` with the formula language of rms. A Poisson model
of the number of pregnancies, with incidence rate ratios:

```{r Glm}
fit_G <- Glm(npreg ~ age + bmi, data = pima, family = poisson)
table_regression(fit_G, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

## `cph()`

The Cox model of rms takes the same spline terms. The example uses
the 312 randomized patients of the Mayo Clinic trial in primary
biliary cholangitis (`survival::pbc`), with death as the event.

```{r cph}
pbc2 <- subset(pbc, !is.na(trt))
pbc2$death <- as.integer(pbc2$status == 2)
pbc2$edema <- factor(pbc2$edema)
ddp <- datadist(pbc2)
options(datadist = "ddp")

fit_cph <- cph(
  Surv(time, death) ~ rcs(age, 4) + log(bili) + albumin + edema,
  data = pbc2, x = TRUE, y = TRUE
)
table_regression(fit_cph, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

The row of bilirubin is labelled `log(bili)`, the term of the
formula, where rms's own printout says `bili`. Its hazard ratio is per
unit of log bilirubin, that is for a bilirubin multiplied by 2.72.

Age is close to linear here: `anova(fit_cph)` gives a Wald χ² of 0.94
on 2 degrees of freedom for its nonlinear terms, p = .63. A single
linear term for age is then the model to report.

[*Survival regression tables*](table-regression-survival.html) covers
the Cox table itself, the cluster-robust variance of `cph()` and the
absolute effects, which are computed for `survival::coxph()` fits
only.

## What spicy refuses for rms fits

A request the fit cannot honor is an explained error.

* Fitters outside the four above: `orm()`, `psm()`, `Gls()`, `Rq()`
  and a formula-less `lrm.fit()`. The message names the supported
  twin where there is one, `survival::survreg()` for `psm()`.
* The term-level test columns, `"partial_chi2"` and `"partial_f"`.
  The joint test of a predictor goes through `nested = TRUE`, as
  above, or through `anova()` of rms.
* `"concordance"` in `show_fit_stats`, defined for `coxph()` fits.
  The indexes of an rms fit are in `fit$stats`.
* The RMST and risk-difference columns of a Cox model, and average
  marginal effects for `cph()`.
* `standardized`. Average marginal effects compare predictors on a
  common scale for `lrm()`, `ols()` and `Glm()`.
* Every `vcov` but `"classical"` and `"CR0"`.

```{r refusal, error = TRUE}
table_regression(orm(glu ~ age + bmi, data = pima))
```

## Presentation-ready output

Everything above renders through the rich output engines. The three
models of age as a `gt` table:

```{r rich, eval = build_rich_tables && have_gt}
pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_regression(
    list(Linear = fit_lin, Categories = fit_cat, Spline = fit_rcs),
    show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
    show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", "aic"),
    output = "gt"
  )
)
```

## References

* Harrell, F. E. (2015). *Regression modeling strategies: With
  applications to linear models, logistic and ordinal regression, and
  survival analysis* (2nd ed.). Springer.
* Nagelkerke, N. J. D. (1991). A note on a general definition of the
  coefficient of determination. *Biometrika*, 78(3), 691--692.
* Tjur, T. (2009). Coefficients of determination in logistic
  regression models—A new proposal: The coefficient of
  discrimination. *The American Statistician*, 63(4), 366--372.
* Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). *Modern applied statistics
  with S* (4th ed.). Springer.
